# Walmart: What Drives Customer Purchases?
```{r init, include=F}
library(ezids)
```

#### - S.M.A.R.T Questions:

Which customer, store, time, promotion, and weather factors are associated with whether a Walmart purchase is an appliance or an electronic product?

This Walmart dataset contains 5000 records of transactions.  Each individual record represents one transaction from a customer.  Each individual record has a variable attached to the transaction representing what type of item was purchased.  That variable is called the category variable and its values are either electronics or appliances.  There are many other variables within our dataset, but we limited our investigation down to 14 variables that could have an association with the category variable.  Our data set was gathered through the free online platform Kaggle.com.  Some analysis that is seen within real world retail companies are studies such as demographic of customers and their locations or seasonal sales trends and promotional effects.  Initially with the background of retail analysis we formatted our first try at the smart question based on aggregations such as total revenue and/or average revenue per transaction.
However, once we did our exploratory data analysis we started to see these 14 variables could have associations with our category variable.  Which led to us abandoning our original smart question, and just working through the exploratory data analysis and the hypothesis testing of all 14 variables.  Once we started to see a more clear answer to our unknown question we were able to put what we were looking for on paper.  It was hard to initially say our smart question due to having so many variables to look at, but once we analyzed all the variables it was easy to formulate our final smart question.  Overall, our research is focussed on finding which individual variables have statistical evidence of an association with the variable category being either electronics or appliances.


# 1. Store Location, Customer Loyalty Level, Payment Method, and Customer Income On Category:

## Author of this section: "Aspen Saplan"

## Set up of dataset walmart:
```{r, echo=TRUE}
#getwd()
walmart = read.csv("Walmart.csv")
walmart$category = as.factor(walmart$category)
walmart$store_location = as.factor(walmart$store_location)
walmart$customer_loyalty_level = as.factor(walmart$customer_loyalty_level)
walmart$payment_method = as.factor(walmart$payment_method)
print(str(walmart$category))
print(str(walmart$store_location))
print(str(walmart$customer_loyalty_level))
print(str(walmart$payment_method))
print(str(walmart$customer_income))
```

The variables that will be focussed on in this section will be store location, customer loyalty level, payment method, and  customer income when comparing to the category variable. 

The three qualitative or factor variables in this section are store location, customer loyalty level, and payment method. Store location is made up of four total locations being Chicago, IL: Dallas, TX; Los Angeles, CA; Miami, FL; New York, NY. Customer loyalty level consists of four total levels being platinum, gold, silver and bronze.  Payment method consists of four total payment options being cash, credit card, debit card, and digital wallet.

#### - Summary statistics of store location:

```{r,echo=TRUE}
summary(walmart$store_location)
```

#### - Summary statistics of customer loyalty level:

```{r,echo=TRUE}
summary(walmart$customer_loyalty_level)
```

#### - Summary statistics of payment method:

```{r,echo=TRUE}
summary(walmart$payment_method)
```

## EDA:

For the following factor variables I used a grouped bar chart with the number of transactions as the Y axis and the variable as the X axis.  I then filled them by which category they were, either appliances or electronics.  

```{r,echo=TRUE}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(walmart, aes(x = store_location, fill = category)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge", color = "black")+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Appliances" = "purple",
    "Electronics" = "red"
  ))+
  labs(title = "Number of Transactions by Store Location and Filled with Category",
    x = "Store Location",
    y = "Number of Transactions",
    fill = "Category")
```

```{r,echo=TRUE}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(walmart, aes(x = customer_loyalty_level, fill = category)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge", color = "black")+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Appliances" = "purple",
    "Electronics" = "red"
  ))+
  labs(title = "Number of Transactions by Customer Loyalty Level and Filled with Category",
    x = "Customer Loyalty Level",
    y = "Number of Transactions",
    fill = "Category")
```

```{r,echo=TRUE}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(walmart, aes(x = payment_method, fill = category)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge", color = "black")+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Appliances" = "purple",
    "Electronics" = "red"
  ))+

    x = "Payment Method",
    y = "Number of Transactions",
    fill = "Category")

Looking at the different grouped bar charts that consist of store location, customer loyalty level, and payment method comparing them to the number of transactions filled by the category variable.  The electronics transactions have a tendency to exceed the appliance transactions for the most part.  There are a few cases such as New York, NY having appliance transactions exceed electronics transactions or the silver customer loyalty level having the same amount of electronic transactions as appliance transactions.  So, there is a pattern of electronics out weighing appliances for when looking at store location, customer loyalty level, and payment method.

The last variable to be explored in this section is customer income.  This variable is numerical so no need to factor it as R will treat this variable correctly. However, I will split appliances and electronics transactions into subsets in order to see the distribution for each category by customer income.

#### - Summary of customer income:

```

#### - Subset of electronics:

print(head(electronics[, c("category", "customer_income")], n=5))
```

```

Looking at both electronics customer income and appliances customer income using a histogram, it suggests that both electronics and appliances have a pretty uniform distribution.  Looking at a boxplot of the two categories shows that they have pretty similar descriptive statistics.  Thus, through the descriptive statistics there is not a huge pattern or trend regarding customer income and category.  The distributions are very similar to each other with no skewing at any value.  While the descriptive statistics such as mean, median, and inter quartile ranges are also similar to each other indicating customer income may not have a huge impact on which category is purchased.

## Sketched answer:

My overall quick sketch of an answer to our question would be that customer income most likely will not have an association to the category variable, while the other categorical variables may have an association with the category variable.

## Hypothesis Testing:

A chi-squared test must be used for the store location, customer loyalty level, and payment method variable when testing for independence with the category variable.  A chi-squared test must be used due to store location, customer loyalty, and payment method being categorical variables and the category variable being categorical variable as well.  First a contingency table has to be made for store location and category, customer loyalty level and category, and payment method and category.

```{r,echo=TRUE}
contableSL = table(walmart$category, walmart$store_location)
xkabledply(contableSL, title="Contingency table for category and store_location within walmart dataset")
```

```{r,echo=TRUE}
contableCLL = table(walmart$category, walmart$customer_loyalty_level)
xkabledply(contableCLL, title="Contingency table for category and customer_loyalty_level within walmart dataset")
```

```{r,echo=TRUE}
contablePM = table(walmart$category, walmart$payment_method)
xkabledply(contablePM, title="Contingency table for category and payment_method within walmart dataset")
```

#### - Test of Independence on category and store_location using contableSL:

Null Hypothesis: Category and store_location are independent

Alternative Hypothesis: Category and store_location are not independent

Alpha = 0.05

```{r, echo=TRUE}
chitestSL = chisq.test(contableSL)
chitestSL
```

After running our chi-squared test on store location and category we can see that our p-value returned is 0.149.  Comparing our p-value(0.149) and our alpha value(0.05) we can see that the p-value is greater than alpha.  Thus, since our p-value is greater than our alpha value we fail to reject the null hypothesis, which provides evidence suggesting that store location and category are independent and have no association. 

#### - Test of Independence on category and customer_loyalty_level using contableCLL:

Null Hypothesis: Category and customer_loyalty_level are independent

Alternative Hypothesis: Category and customer_loyalty_level are not independent

Alpha = 0.05

```{r, echo=TRUE}
chitestCLL = chisq.test(contableCLL)
chitestCLL
```

After running our chi-squared test on customer loyalty level and category we can see that our p-value returned is 0.3872.  Comparing our p-value(0.3872) and our alpha value(0.05) we can see that the p-value is greater than alpha.  Thus, since our p-value is greater than our alpha value we fail to reject the null hypothesis, which provides evidence suggesting that customer loyalty level and category are independent and have no association. 

#### - Test of Independence on category and payment_method using contablePM:

Null Hypothesis: Category and payment_method are independent

Alternative Hypothesis: Category and payment_method are not independent

Alpha = 0.05
```{r, echo=TRUE}
chitestPM = chisq.test(contablePM)
chitestPM
```

After running our chi-squared test on payment method and category we can see that our p-value returned is 0.8445.  Comparing our p-value(0.8445) and our alpha value(0.05) we can see that the p-value is greater than alpha.  Thus, since our p-value is greater than our alpha value we fail to reject the null hypothesis, which provides evidence suggesting that payment method and category are independent and have no association.

For the customer income variable I started by separating appliance transactions and electronics transactions into two subsets.  Knowing that customer income is a numerical variable I know that a two sample t-test is needed for this hypothesis test.

#### - T-Test of customer_income and category:

Customer_income Null Hypothesis: means are equal for appliances and electronics

Customer_income Alternative Hypothesis: means are not equal for appliances and electronics

Alpha = 0.05

```{r,echo=TRUE}
ttestCI = t.test(appliances$customer_income, electronics$customer_income)
ttestCI
```

After running the t-test on appliances customer income and electronics customer income we can see that our p-value returned is 0.1725.  Comparing our p-value(0.1725) and our alpha value(0.05) we can see that the p-value is greater than alpha.  Thus, since our p-value is greater than our alpha we fail to reject the null hypothesis.  So, the evidence does not suggest that a higher or lower income is associated with purchasing electronics over appliances and vice versa.

## Outcome:

Through different hypothesis testing on these variables of store location, customer loyalty level, payment method, and customer income.  The data suggests that all of our variables are independent or share the same population mean when compared across the variable category.

# 2. Day of the week, holidays, and type of weather considered against total sales and sales by category

## Author of this section: Alex Rizzo-Banks


Each of the following variables will be compared against the variable "category" to tell us if the given variables influence preference toward appliances or electronics or if they show a dependence between number of transactions (also mentioned as "sales" herein):

#### A. "weekday" is a character variable with the days of the week as levels. We have used the factor() function to order them 1-7 starting with "Monday".

``` {r}
walmart$weekday = factor(walmart$weekday, levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"), ordered = TRUE)
str(walmart$weekday)
```


#### B. "holiday_indicator" is a binary logical variable that was recorded as TRUE for transactions taking place on a holiday.

```{r}
str(walmart$holiday_indicator)
```

#### C. "weather_conditions" is a character variable with four levels: "Sunny", "Cloudy", "Rainy", and "Stormy". These are not ordered.

``` {r}
walmart$weather_conditions = factor(walmart$weather_conditions, levels = c("Stormy", "Rainy", "Sunny", "Cloudy"), ordered = FALSE)
unique(walmart$weather_conditions)
```

## EDA

First, Let's expand the "holiday_indicator" category next to the transaction dates to figure out if these are only national holidays or a larger set.

```{r}
HOLIDAYS = data.frame(walmart$transaction_date, walmart$holiday_indicator)
xkabledplyhead(HOLIDAYS, rows = 15)
```

We can see from the HOLIDAYS DataFrame that these holidays likely refer to promotional periods run by Walmart surrounding national and other holidays such as July 4th, Juneteenth, etc, rather than single days. However, we would need more data or another document to confirm this, such as a Walmart internal schedule or historical list of holidays observed by the store (These days are obviously not days where the store closes, as they are days where transactions took place).

### Bar Charts
```{r}
ggplot(walmart, aes(x = weekday, fill = category)) + geom_bar(position = "dodge") + labs(x = "Day of the week", y = "Number of Transactions",title = "Sales on different days of the week", fill= "Category")
ggplot(walmart, aes(x = holiday_indicator,  fill = category)) + geom_bar(position = "dodge") + labs(x = "Holiday vs. Non-holiday", y = "Number of Transactions", title = "Sales on holidays vs. normal days", fill = "Category", )
ggplot(walmart, aes(x = weather_conditions, fill = category)) + geom_bar(position = "dodge") + labs(x = "Weather", y = "Transactions", title = "Sales on days with different kinds of weather", fill = "Category")
```

There is no clear trend indicating that any of the three qualifiers affect the sales of electronics versus appliances, though we do see that electronics noticeably outsell appliances on Mondays. Overall, electronics sell better but not by much. Next we'll use Chi tests to confirm whether these variables have an impact on category value or not.

## Hypothesis Testing

First, we'll need to create a contingency table for each variable paired with category.

```{r}
contabwk = table(walmart$category, walmart$weekday)
contabhol = table(walmart$category, walmart$holiday_indicator)
contabwthr = table(walmart$category, walmart$weather_conditions)
```

#### Contingency Table for Category and Day of the Week
```{r}
xkabledply(contabwk, title = "Contingency Table: Category + Day of the Week")
```


#### Contingency Table for Category and Holiday Indicator
```{r}
xkabledply(contabhol, title = "Contingency Table: Category + Holiday Indicator")
```


#### Contingency Table for Category and Type of Weather
```{r}
xkabledply(contabwthr, title = "Contingency Table: Category + Type of Weather")
```


### A. Testing Day of the Week

For (A), our alpha value is 0.05. Our null hypothesis is that day of the week has no impact on whether electronics or appliances sell better than the other. Our alternative hypothesis is that the day of the week will have some correlation with the category that sells better.
```{r}
chitestwk = chisq.test(contabwk)
chitestwk
```

### B. Testing Holidays vs. Non-holidays

For (B) our alpha value will be 0.05 and our null hypothesis is that the day of sale being holiday does not impact whether electronics or appliances outsells the other. Our alternative hypothesis is that the presence of a holiday or a non-holiday will show some impact on which level of the category variable records more transactions.
```{r}
chitesthol = chisq.test(contabhol)
chitesthol
```

### C. Testing Type of Weather

For (C) our alpha value will be 0.05 and our null hypothesis is that the type of weather has no impact on whether electronics or appliances sells better that day. Our alternative hypothesis is that the type of whether will show some impact on which level of the category variable records more transactions.
```{r}
chitestwthr = chisq.test(contabwthr)
chitestwthr
```

### 2 - Conclusions

For variable A - day of the week, we report a p-value of 0.25. Since this is higher than our alpha level, we fail to reject the null hypothesis; in other words, there does not appear to be any correlation between the day of the week and the strength of appliance sales vs. electronics sales.

For variable B - holiday presence, we report a p-value of 0.89. This is similarly higher than our alpha level, so we once again fail to reject the null hypothesis; whether or not a transaction takes place on a Walmart-recorded holiday does not seem to influence whether that purchase is more likely to be an appliance or electronics.

Finally, for variable C - type of weather, we report a p-value of 0.74. Once again, this value is higher than our alpha level and we fail to reject our null hypothesis. There does not appear to be any correlation between the type of weather and the category of device that a customer chooses to purchase.

#Hypothesis testing using chi-square test of independence and welch t-tests.
```{r}
t.test(unit_price ~ category, data = walmart)

t.test(quantity_sold ~ category, data = walmart)

t.test(customer_age ~ category, data = walmart)

```
Null hypothesis for the t-test: mean unit price of appliances is equal to the mean unit price of electronics. p-value is more than 0.05 so its fails to reject it. For the second test the null hypothesis states that the mean quantity sold of appliances is the equal to the mean quantity sold of electronics. The null hypothesis for the third t-test is mean customer age in appliances is the same as the mean customer age in electronics.The t-tests were used to show any significant differences in unit_price,quantity sold, customer age, and revenue within the the two categories and they all seem to fail to reject the null hypothesis. There isn't a difference in three of the tests. However customer age and category accept the alternate hypothesis. There's disparity in the age groups within the two categories. 


```{r}

contable_gender = table(walmart$category, walmart$customer_gender)
chisq.test(contable_gender)

```
The first code creates a contingency table, which shows how many observations fall into a combination of categories and customer_gender. A chi-square test of independence is used to show whether gender and categories are independent of each other. This means that the null hypothesis would be that gender and category are independent of each other and that both categories have equal distributions of gender. Since 0.631 is higher than 0.5, we fail to reject the null hypothesis

```{r, echo=TRUE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE)
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(janitor)
library(effsize)
```

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# Make sure factors are clean
walmart <- walmart %>%
  mutate(
    category = as.factor(category),
    promotion_applied = as.factor(promotion_applied),
    promotion_type = as.factor(promotion_type)
  )
```


# Create binary category indicator for t-tests:

# 1 = Electronics, 0 = Appliances
```{r, echo=TRUE}
walmart <- walmart %>%
  mutate(category_bin = if_else(category == "Electronics", 1, 0))
```


# Graph: proportion of Electronics by promotion_applied
```{r, echo=TRUE}
walmart %>%
  group_by(promotion_applied) %>%
  summarise(prop_electronics = mean(category_bin),
            n = n(),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = promotion_applied, 
             y = prop_electronics, 
             fill = promotion_applied)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#4E79A7",
                               "TRUE"  = "#E15759")) +
  labs(
    title = "Proportion of Electronics Transactions by Promotion Applied",
    x = "Promotion Applied",
    y = "Proportion Electronics"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The bar chart displays the proportion of Electronics transactions among transactions with and without promotions. The proportions are nearly identical across both groups, suggesting that applying a promotion does not meaningfully shift transactions toward either Electronics or Appliances.

# t-test: does the proportion of Electronics differ by promotion_applied"

```{r, echo=TRUE}
t.test(category_bin ~ promotion_applied, data = walmart)
```

Hypotheses

Null Hypothesis (H0):
The proportion of Electronics transactions is the same for transactions with and without promotions.

Alternative Hypothesis (H1):
The proportion of Electronics transactions differs between transactions with and without promotions.


The Welch two-sample t-test shows no statistically significant difference in the proportion of Electronics transactions between transactions with and without promotions (p = 0.578). The estimated proportions are 52.1% for transactions without promotions and 51.3% for transactions with promotions. The 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating that the true difference in proportions may be zero.

Overall, the data provide no evidence that applying a promotion changes the likelihood that a transaction belongs to the Electronics category rather than Appliances.


# Graph: quantity_sold by category
```{r, echo=TRUE}
ggplot(walmart, aes(x = category, y = quantity_sold)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.08) +
  labs(
    title = "Quantity Sold per Transaction by Category",
    x = "Category",
    y = "Quantity Sold"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r, echo=TRUE}
walmart %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_quantity = mean(quantity_sold),
    sd_quantity = sd(quantity_sold),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

The average number of units purchased per transaction is nearly identical across categories. Appliances transactions have a mean of 2.97 units, while Electronics transactions have a mean of 3.00 units. The standard deviations are also very similar (1.41 and 1.43, respectively), indicating comparable variability in purchase behavior. Overall, there is no meaningful difference in the number of items purchased per transaction between the two categories.

# t-test: does mean quantity differ by category

```{r, echo=TRUE}
t.test(quantity_sold ~ category, data = walmart)
```


Null Hypothesis (H0):
The mean quantity sold per transaction is the same for Appliances and Electronics.

Alternative Hypothesis (H1):
The mean quantity sold per transaction differs between Appliances and Electronics.

The Welch two-sample t-test shows no statistically significant difference in the average number of units purchased per transaction between Appliances and Electronics (p = 0.492). Appliances transactions have a mean of 2.97 units, while Electronics transactions have a mean of 3.00 units. The 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating that the true difference in means may be zero. Therefore, there is no statistical evidence that customers purchase more units per transaction in one category compared to the other.
